description: I’m a Python developer and EdTech specialist leading TEAM Joule Detectives for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. I build open-source tools that process NASA POWER satellite data (solar, wind, temperature, and rainfall) to forecast climate trends and support off-grid energy resilience.
summary: TEAM Joule Detectives developed an open-source, interactive Python web application that transforms NASA POWER Earth observation datasets (2015–2025) into actionable climate intelligence for local renewable energy autonomy. Addressing the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, our platform lets any user select a location via city search or interactive map to evaluate solar radiation, wind speed, temperature, and precipitation in real time. Using linear regression (SciPy), the tool calculates statistical significance ($p < 0.05$) to distinguish real climate trends from annual noise and projects resource trajectories to 2030 through dynamic 2D and 3D charts. Built with zero login barriers and mobile accessibility, it matters because communities and off-grid sites can download lightweight .CSV records and activate Offline Contingency Mode to plan solar or wind power resilience even during grid or internet outages.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Joule Detectives (named after the International System unit of energy, the Joule, and the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge) is an open-source, interactive Python web application that converts raw NASA POWER Earth observation datasets (2015–2025)—sourced from CERES and MERRA-2—into actionable renewable energy and climate intelligence. Users enter any city or click directly on an interactive global map to retrieve exact coordinates (latitude and longitude) and analyze four core variables in real time: all-sky surface solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN), wind speed at 10 meters (WS10M), surface air temperature at 2 meters (T2M), and corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR). Using linear regression (SciPy), the engine calculates decade-level trends, tests statistical significance ($p < 0.05$) to separate real climate shifts from annual variability, and generates 2030 resource projections through dual-axis 2D charts and interactive 3D multivariable trajectories.

Key Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Democratized Access for Non-Technical Users: Anyone—regardless of age or technical background—can access the web app from a smartphone or computer with zero registration, login, or paywall barriers.
  • Grid & Internet Outage Resilience: Users can export official NASA records in lightweight .CSV format with one click and switch on Offline Contingency Mode, allowing rural communities, emergency responders, and off-grid sites to evaluate solar or wind autonomy even when power grids or internet connections fail.
  • Open-Source Replicability: Published openly on GitHub, the codebase empowers educators, students, and local planners worldwide to replicate, audit, and adapt the tool for local energy planning.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Programming Language & Scientific Libraries: Python 3, pandas, NumPy, SciPy (linear regression and $p$-value statistical testing), and Requests.
  • Web Framework & Interactive Visualization: Streamlit (deployed publicly on Streamlit Community Cloud), Plotly (2D dual-axis climate charts and 3D solar vs. wind trajectories), and Folium / streamlit-folium (OpenStreetMap interactive geolocation with coordinate capture).
  • Data & Collaboration Ecosystem: NASA Langley Research Center POWER API, OpenStreetMap Nominatim Geocoding API, GitHub & GitHub Codespaces for open-source version control, and Google Workspace for project documentation and presentation design.

Creativity & Design Factors Considered Rather than building another static climate dashboard, our team combined statistical trend validation ($p < 0.05$) with practical off-grid survival and hardware-free accessibility. In designing the platform, we prioritized: (1) scientific honesty, clearly labeling 2030 forecasts as linear extrapolations over 11-year satellite baselines; (2) universal usability, pairing a high-contrast aerospace dark interface with single-click .CSV caching for low-bandwidth or disconnected environments; and (3) educational clarity, translating complex Earth system telemetry into clear decisions on whether solar or wind infrastructure is most viable at any location on Earth.
